_note: Events measured in the study. Times are local to the origin unless marked UTC.

newspaper_events.label: Death of George Washington
newspaper_events.context: Washington died at Mount Vernon, his home on the Potomac, late on a Saturday evening. The news travelled by horse and by ship.

newspaper_events.label: Treaty of Ghent signed
newspaper_events.context: The treaty crossed the Atlantic on HMS Favorite, which anchored off Sandy Hook, New York, on 11 February 1815. While it was at sea, the Battle of New Orleans was fought on 8 January. New Orleans itself heard of the peace in mid-March.
newspaper_events.phrase: the Treaty of Ghent was signed

newspaper_events.label: Death of Andrew Jackson
newspaper_events.carrier: mail by steamboat, stage and rail
newspaper_events.context: Jackson died at the Hermitage, his home outside Nashville. The first telegraph line, between Washington and Baltimore, had opened the year before.
newspaper_events.reject_near: without foundation|unfounded|not yet|premature|contradict|not dead|not true|false report|sir richard|richard d|montreal

newspaper_events.label: Death of Zachary Taylor
newspaper_events.context: Taylor died in the White House after a short illness. Telegraph lines now linked many eastern cities, but not yet the West.

newspaper_events.label: Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
newspaper_events.context: Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre and died the next morning. The telegraph had reached California in 1861.

newspaper_events.label: Sinking of the Titanic
newspaper_events.origin: North Atlantic, 600 km south of Newfoundland
newspaper_events.context: The ship struck the iceberg at 11:40 p.m. ship's time, 9:38 p.m. in New York, and sank at 2:20 a.m. The first news came by wireless.

newspaper_events.label: Attack on Pearl Harbor
newspaper_events.context: The attack began at 7:48 on a Sunday morning in Hawaii, early afternoon on the East Coast. Radio carried the news first; many papers printed extra editions.

newspaper_events.label: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
newspaper_events.context: Kennedy was shot in his motorcade in Dallas and died half an hour later. The first wire bulletin went out four minutes after the shots, and television broke into its programmes soon after.

web_events.label: Notre-Dame de Paris fire
web_events.context: The fire alarm sounded at 18:18, but the fire itself was found only at 18:43, after a second alarm. The spire fell at 19:50.

_note_windows: Search windows were shortened for speed where it cannot change the result: a paper is lost only if its first report fell after the window closed. Titanic and Pearl Harbor use front pages only; a paper that ran the story inside first is placed at its first front-page report, which can only make the news look slower.
_note_trust: trust_search: the search terms only occur once the event has happened, so the Library's own text match confirms the paper. One page per paper is still read to keep a quotation; a paper whose quote can't be matched is kept and flagged 'search'. 'after-first-day' applies this only after the event day; same-day pages are read in full.
_note_floor: first_valid is the earliest date a report can be genuine. For Ghent it is the evening HMS Favorite anchored off Sandy Hook, 11 February 1815; earlier 'peace signed' items in American papers were rumours or other treaties.
_note_reject: reject_near: a match is skipped when these words appear within 300 characters of it, and reading moves on to the next match. For Ghent it removes a treaty with Indian tribes reported the same week. For Jackson it removes reports of his death that were denied as rumours, and the death of Sir Richard Jackson in Montreal the same week. A rumour mention is also skipped unless the passage says it was confirmed.
_note_web: Web era: GDELT Global Knowledge Graph, English and translated files, from public_utc for 48 hours. A site counts at its first article whose address, title and extracted names, places and themes meet every rule in match. scripts/web_published.py then replaces GDELT's time with the publication time on the article's own page where there is one. Death words must be in the address or title, so articles about the Queen's health before the announcement do not count. Batches stamped at or before the event are skipped, because a batch holds what GDELT found in the 15 minutes before its stamp. For Elizabeth II, articles that ask what would happen if or when she died, or that describe the funeral plans, do not count. For Notre-Dame, articles are counted from 18:43 Paris time, when the fire was found; the clock still starts at the first alarm, 18:18. For the earthquake, a word for earthquake must appear in the article's address or title, because GDELT's themes alone also matched unrelated pages.
